title: ⭐⭐ Practice: the habit that stopped, the aim behind the act

questions.prompt: A youth centre in El Kef prints a page of short life stories. Complete both gaps: "Hedi left his evening class in December to take a full-time job, and for weeks he felt ___ the teacher who had found him a place in it. Two years later he is still at the workshop, and he says he has grown ___ the smell of sawdust and the noise of the machines."

options.text: envious of / proud of
proud of / relieved about
guilty towards / fond of
relieved about / envious of

questions.explanation: "guilty towards / fond of" fills the two gaps. You feel guilty towards somebody when you believe you have let that person down, and Hedi walked out of the class the teacher had found him a place in, so that is the word for those first weeks. And you grow fond of a thing you have come to like over time, which is what two years of sawdust and machine noise have done to him. "envious of / proud of" puts envy where there is nothing to envy, since nobody in the story has what Hedi wanted, and then makes him proud of a smell, when pride is what you feel about something that is your own doing. "proud of / relieved about" fails on both gaps for those same two reasons, and relief needs a worry that lifts, which no workshop noise ever provided. And "relieved about / envious of" opens with the feeling you have when the thing you feared does not happen, which is not what walking out of a class produces, and closes by making him envy a smell.

questions.prompt: Read this note a pupil wrote about her neighbour. "Aunt Zohra opened her own tailor's shop in Nabeul at twenty-four. For thirty years she sewed wedding dresses for the whole street. She sold the shop and the machines in 2021. She mends her grandchildren's clothes every week." The pupil wants to rewrite one of these four facts with "used to", and only one of them will take it. Which fact?

options.text: She sewed wedding dresses for the whole street.
She opened her own tailor's shop in Nabeul at twenty-four.
She mends her grandchildren's clothes every week.
She sold the shop and the machines in 2021.

questions.explanation: "She sewed wedding dresses for the whole street." is the one: it lasted thirty years, it was repeated week after week, and the shop has been sold, so the habit is over — which is exactly what used to says, and the note becomes She used to sew wedding dresses for the whole street. "She opened her own tailor's shop in Nabeul at twenty-four." happened once, on one day; a single event takes the past simple and never used to, whatever its date. "She sold the shop and the machines in 2021." is a single event as well, and it even carries its year, which closes the question. And "She mends her grandchildren's clothes every week." is a habit she still has today, written in the present; used to would send it back into the past, and the note says that it is going on.

questions.prompt: A school magazine in Gafsa is reporting on the book sale its club ran last month. The editor has four lines in front of her. Three of them name something the club was aiming at before the sale began; the fourth names no aim at all: it reports what the sale actually produced. Which line reports what the sale produced?

options.text: The club sold the books at half price so that the youngest pupils could afford them.
The club opened the stall at seven so that the boarders could buy before class.
The club kept twenty copies aside so that the library could replace its worn ones.
The club sold the books at half price, so the last box was empty by four.

questions.explanation: "The club sold the books at half price, so the last box was empty by four." is the line that reports: a comma and so on its own join a fact to the fact that followed it, and an empty box at four o'clock is what happened, not what anybody wanted. The three other lines all open a clause with so that, and so that names what was wanted before the act, without ever saying whether it worked: "The club sold the books at half price so that the youngest pupils could afford them." gives the reason the price was fixed low and leaves open whether the youngest pupils came at all. "The club opened the stall at seven so that the boarders could buy before class." gives the reason for the hour, not what the hour produced. And "The club kept twenty copies aside so that the library could replace its worn ones." gives the reason twenty copies were held back, and the library may still not have collected them. One word is the whole difference: so that plus a clause is an aim, so on its own after a comma is a result.

questions.prompt: A garage in Menzel Bourguiba offered Nizar a fortnight of work experience in July, and he answered no the same evening. The garage has taken somebody else since, and he has found nothing else all autumn. He is talking about it to his sister now. Which sentence says what he thinks?

options.text: I should have refused that fortnight in the garage.
I shouldn't have refused that fortnight in the garage.
I shouldn't refuse that fortnight in the garage.
I didn't have to refuse that fortnight in the garage at all.

questions.explanation: "I shouldn't have refused that fortnight in the garage." is what he thinks: shouldn't have says that the thing was done and ought not to have been, which is exactly his case, and the past participle refused puts the whole matter beyond repair. "I should have refused that fortnight in the garage." turns the facts round: should have says that the thing was not done, so the line would mean that he accepted the fortnight and now wishes he had said no. "I shouldn't refuse that fortnight in the garage." is advice about an offer still on the table; this one was answered in July and the place has gone, and a present modal cannot reach a decision that is over. And "I didn't have to refuse that fortnight in the garage at all." only says that nothing obliged him to say no, which is true and beside the point: an absence of obligation is not a regret, and the sentence passes no judgement on the choice.

questions.prompt: Hichem has spent four months at the same counter, doing the same three tasks every morning, and this week he has started looking for something else. Complete the line he writes to a friend: "By the end of March I was fed up ___ the same three things every day."

options.text: of doing
to do
with doing
with to do

questions.explanation: "with doing" is the form: fed up takes the preposition with, and after a preposition an English verb goes into its -ing form, so the expression is always fed up with doing something. "of doing" chooses the wrong preposition, the one many learners hear in fed up of; the -ing form is right, the little word in front of it is not. "with to do" keeps the right preposition and then breaks the rule that follows it: after with, English never puts an infinitive. And "to do" drops the preposition altogether, which is what your own language would let you do; in English fed up is never followed directly by a verb.

questions.prompt: Emna's class has to hand in an interview, and her first question is for a retired railway clerk from El Kef. She wants to ask him whether Sunday duty was a regular part of his work in those years. Which question does she write?

options.text: Do you use to work on Sundays?
Have you used to work on Sundays?
Did you used to work on Sundays?
Did you use to work on Sundays?

questions.explanation: "Did you use to work on Sundays?" is the question: the interrogative of used to is built with did, and did already carries the past, so the verb behind it loses its -d and comes back to use. "Did you used to work on Sundays?" marks the past twice over, once on did and once on used, where English marks it only once; it is the mistake this form attracts most often. "Do you use to work on Sundays?" puts the question in the present, where it would ask about the clerk's working life today, and he has retired. And "Have you used to work on Sundays?" borrows the auxiliary of the present perfect, which used to never takes; the two forms carry opposite messages, since the present perfect ties the past to now and used to leaves it in the past.
